title: Probability & Statistics
subject: Probability & Statistics
summary: Probability from counting and Bayes' rule through the normal, Poisson and exponential distributions, the central limit theorem, maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, then the frequentist toolkit of the analytical lab: confidence intervals, t-tests, chi-square, least-squares calibration curves and error propagation. Blitzstein and Hwang carry the probability; OpenIntro carries the applied statistics. Chemistry hooks throughout: counting statistics in detectors and mass spectrometers, isotope patterns, first-order decay, Bayesian spectral assignment and calibration-curve uncertainty. The groundwork for the probabilistic view of machine learning in A1 and for statistical mechanics.

units.title: Probability and Counting
units.summary: Sample spaces, the naive definition, counting with the multiplication rule and binomial coefficients, and the axioms that make probability work when outcomes are not equally likely.

lessons.title: Sample Spaces and the Naive Definition
objectives: Write the sample space for an experiment (coin tosses, drawing vials from a rack) and express events as subsets built with union, intersection and complement.
Compute probabilities with the naive definition and state exactly when it is valid (finite sample space, equally likely outcomes).

lessons.title: Counting: Multiplication Rule, Binomial Coefficients and Story Proofs
objectives: Count ordered and unordered samples with and without replacement (the four entries of the sampling table), e.g. the number of ways to pick 3 of 12 NMR tubes.
Prove a combinatorial identity such as n·C(n-1,k-1) = k·C(n,k) by a story proof (counting the same set two ways).
Count isomers or substitution patterns with binomial coefficients (e.g. placements of 2 deuteriums on 6 equivalent sites) and recognise when symmetry makes outcomes non-equally-likely.

Class 1b reading notes: Counting and Sets

lessons.title: The Axioms of Probability and Inclusion-Exclusion
objectives: State the two axioms of probability and derive P(A^c) = 1 - P(A) and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B) from them.
Apply inclusion-exclusion to three or more events (e.g. the matching problem) and use complements to solve 'at least one' problems such as the birthday problem.
keyEquations: P\left(\bigcup_j A_j\right) = \sum_j P(A_j) \text{ for disjoint } A_j

units.title: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule
units.summary: Updating probabilities on evidence: conditional probability, the law of total probability and Bayes' rule, applied to diagnostic tests and to assigning a spectrum to a candidate structure.

lessons.title: Conditional Probability
objectives: Compute P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) from a two-way table or tree diagram and explain it as restricting the sample space to B.
Use the multiplication rule P(A∩B) = P(B)P(A|B) to compute the probability of a sequence of events (e.g. drawing two contaminated samples in a row).
keyEquations: P(A_1\cap\cdots\cap A_n) = P(A_1)P(A_2\mid A_1)\cdots P(A_n\mid A_1,\dots,A_{n-1})

lectures.title: Statistics 110: Probability (full lecture playlist)
Lecture 4: Conditional Probability

demoIdeas: Two overlapping event regions on a unit square: clicking 'condition on B' rescales B to fill the square and shows P(A|B) as the shaded share.

lessons.title: Bayes' Rule, Total Probability and Diagnostic Tests
objectives: Compute P(B) by the law of total probability over a partition, and invert conditionals with Bayes' rule.

Compute the positive predictive value of a test from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence (e.g. a drug screen or a qualitative spot test) and explain why a rare condition gives many false positives.

readings.title: Bayes' rule and the law of total probability

lectures.title: Lecture 5: Conditioning Continued, Law of Total Probability
Class 3 reading notes: Conditional Probability, Independence, Bayes' Theorem

demoIdeas: A 1000-person icon array with sliders for prevalence, sensitivity and specificity; true/false positives recolour live and the PPV updates.

lessons.title: Bayes in Odds Form: Assigning a Spectrum
objectives: Rewrite Bayes' rule as posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio, and update the odds sequentially for independent pieces of evidence.

Assign posterior probabilities to 3–4 candidate structures from a prior (synthetic route plausibility) and the likelihood of each observed spectral feature (an IR carbonyl band, an NMR multiplet, an MS fragment), stating the independence assumption used.
Explain why conditional probabilities given E obey all the probability rules, so evidence can be applied one piece at a time.

lectures.title: Class 12b reading notes: Bayesian Updating: Odds

lessons.title: Independence and Conditional Independence
objectives: Test two or three events for independence and pairwise vs. full independence from their probabilities.

Give an example where events are conditionally independent given C but dependent unconditionally (two instruments reading the same unknown sample), and explain why this matters when combining evidence.
keyEquations: P(A\cap B\mid C) = P(A\mid C)P(B\mid C)

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Conditional Probability (independence)

lessons.title: Conditioning as a Tool; Pitfalls and Paradoxes
objectives: Solve the Monty Hall problem by conditioning on the host's action, and solve recursive problems by first-step analysis (conditioning on the first event).
Explain Simpson's paradox with a two-catalyst yield table where one catalyst wins in every substrate class yet loses overall, and name the prosecutor's fallacy (confusing P(E|H) with P(H|E)).

lectures.title: Lecture 6: Monty Hall, Simpson's Paradox

units.title: Discrete Random Variables
units.summary: Random variables, PMFs and CDFs, the binomial and hypergeometric models, expectation and variance, and the Poisson distribution behind counting statistics in detectors, mass spectrometers and scintillation counters.

lessons.title: Random Variables, PMFs and CDFs
objectives: Define a random variable as a function on the sample space and distinguish the r.v. from its distribution.
Write the PMF and CDF of a discrete r.v. and check validity (non-negative, sums to 1; CDF non-decreasing, right-continuous, limits 0 and 1).

lectures.title: Statistics 110: Probability (full lecture playlist)
Class 4a reading notes: Discrete Random Variables

lessons.title: Bernoulli, Binomial and Hypergeometric
objectives: Recognise binomial stories (n independent trials, fixed p) and compute binomial probabilities, e.g. the number of 13C atoms in a molecule with 10 carbons at 1.1% natural abundance (the M+1 peak).
Distinguish sampling with replacement (binomial) from without replacement (hypergeometric), e.g. defective vials in a lot of 50, and state when the binomial approximates the hypergeometric.

lessons.title: Expectation, Linearity and Indicator Variables
objectives: Compute E[X] for a discrete r.v. from its PMF and use linearity E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even for dependent X and Y.
Use indicator r.v.s and the fundamental bridge E[I_A] = P(A) to find expectations of counts (e.g. expected number of matches, expected number of sites substituted).
Derive the mean of the binomial and geometric distributions by linearity.

lessons.title: LOTUS and Variance
objectives: Compute E[g(X)] with LOTUS without finding the distribution of g(X).
Compute Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 and use Var(aX+b) = a^2 Var(X) and additivity of variance for independent r.v.s, e.g. the variance of a binomial as a sum of Bernoullis.

lessons.title: The Poisson Distribution and Counting Statistics
objectives: Derive the Poisson as the limit of the binomial with n large, p small, np = λ, and state its mean and variance (both λ).

Explain counting statistics: a detector recording N counts has standard deviation √N, so relative precision is 1/√N; compute the counts needed for 1% precision and the uncertainty of a background-subtracted count.
Decide whether a Poisson model fits a counting experiment (ion counts in an MS bin, scintillation counts, photon counts) and name what breaks it (dead time, detector saturation).

lectures.title: Lecture 11: The Poisson Distribution

demoIdeas: Photon-counting detector: set the count rate and integration time, collect repeated readings, and compare the histogram with the Poisson PMF and its √N error bar.
Binomial(n, λ/n) vs Poisson(λ): increase n and watch the two PMFs merge.

units.title: Continuous Random Variables
units.summary: Densities and CDFs, the uniform, normal and exponential distributions, the Poisson process that ties exponential waiting times (radioactive and first-order decay) to Poisson counts, and moment generating functions.

lessons.title: Probability Density Functions and the Uniform
objectives: Compute probabilities as areas under a PDF, find a PDF from a CDF by differentiation, and explain why P(X = x) = 0 for a continuous r.v.
Compute the mean and variance of a continuous r.v. by integration, using the Uniform(a, b) as the worked case (e.g. the reading error of a pipette graduation).

Class 5b reading notes: Continuous Random Variables
Class 6a reading notes: Continuous Random Variables: Expectation and Variance

lessons.title: The Normal Distribution
objectives: Standardise X ~ N(μ, σ^2) to Z and compute probabilities and quantiles with Φ, including the 68-95-99.7 rule.
Use the facts that a linear function of a normal is normal and a sum of independent normals is normal (means add, variances add).
Explain why replicate lab measurements are often modelled as normal, and when that fails (outliers, skewed concentrations, values near a detection limit).

lectures.title: Class 5c reading notes: Gallery of Continuous Random Variables

lessons.title: The Exponential Distribution and Decay
objectives: State the Exponential(λ) PDF, CDF, mean 1/λ and variance 1/λ^2, and connect λ to a half-life (t_1/2 = ln 2 / λ) and to a first-order rate constant.
Prove the memoryless property and interpret it for radioactive nuclei and for single molecules undergoing first-order reaction (no ageing).

lessons.title: The Poisson Process: Counts and Waiting Times
objectives: Define a Poisson process of rate λ and show that the count in time t is Poisson(λt) while the gaps between arrivals are i.i.d. Exponential(λ).

lessons.title: Moments and Moment Generating Functions
objectives: Interpret mean, variance, skewness and kurtosis as summaries of a distribution's location, spread, asymmetry and tails.
Find the MGF of the Bernoulli, Poisson and normal, generate moments by differentiating at t = 0, and use MGFs to show that a sum of independent Poissons is Poisson.

units.title: Joint Distributions, Covariance and Error Propagation
units.summary: Several random quantities at once: joint, marginal and conditional distributions, covariance and correlation, and the variance of functions of measured quantities, the theory behind the propagation-of-error formulas used in lab reports.

lessons.title: Joint, Marginal and Conditional Distributions
objectives: Find marginal and conditional distributions from a joint PMF table or joint PDF, and test independence by factorisation.
Compute E[g(X, Y)] with 2D LOTUS, e.g. the expected product of two measured quantities.

lessons.title: Covariance and Correlation
objectives: Compute Cov(X, Y) and Corr(X, Y), use bilinearity of covariance, and derive Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y).
Explain why zero correlation does not imply independence, and why correlated errors (a shared calibration standard, a shared balance) must not be added as if independent.

lessons.title: Propagation of Uncertainty
objectives: Derive the variance of a linear combination aX + bY (including the covariance term) and apply it to a difference of masses or a background-subtracted signal.

Derive the first-order (delta-method) propagation formula σ_f^2 ≈ Σ (∂f/∂x_i)^2 σ_i^2 from a Taylor expansion, and apply it to a concentration c = A/(εl) and to a ratio or product (relative errors add in quadrature).

units.title: Inequalities and Limit Theorems
units.summary: Why averaging replicates works: Markov and Chebyshev bounds, the law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, and the chi-square and Student-t distributions that small lab samples need.

lessons.title: Markov, Chebyshev and the Law of Large Numbers
objectives: Apply Markov's and Chebyshev's inequalities to bound tail probabilities using only a mean (and variance).
State the weak law of large numbers, prove it from Chebyshev, and explain what it does and does not promise about the sample mean of replicate measurements.

lessons.title: The Central Limit Theorem

units.title: Estimation and Maximum Likelihood
units.summary: Turning data into parameter estimates: bias, variance and mean squared error of estimators, maximum likelihood, standard errors from the curvature of the log-likelihood, and inverse-variance weighting of measurements.

lessons.title: Estimators: Bias, Variance and MSE
objectives: Define an estimator and compute its bias, variance and MSE, and show MSE = bias^2 + variance.
Show that the sample mean is unbiased and that the sample variance needs the n-1 divisor to be unbiased.

units.title: Bayesian Inference
units.summary: Probability as a state of knowledge about parameters: updating discrete and continuous priors, the Beta-Binomial, Gamma-Poisson and Normal-Normal conjugate pairs, credible intervals, and how Bayesian and frequentist answers compare.

lessons.title: The Beta Prior and Beta-Binomial Conjugacy
objectives: Describe the Beta(a, b) family, its mean a/(a+b), and how a and b act as pseudo-counts of prior successes and failures.

project.title: Counting Statistics and a Calibration Curve, End to End
project.summary: A Python analysis of a simulated (or the learner's own) analytical data set: Poisson counting data from a detector and a five-standard calibration curve. The learner estimates rates by maximum likelihood and Bayes, tests the Poisson model, fits the calibration line by ordinary and weighted least squares, and reports an unknown's concentration with a propagated uncertainty checked by Monte Carlo and the bootstrap.
goals: Simulate Poisson counting data and verify the √N rule, the MLE of the rate and a chi-square goodness-of-fit test.
Estimate a low background rate with a Gamma-Poisson posterior and compare the credible interval with the frequentist interval.
Fit a calibration curve by OLS and WLS, inspect residuals and the reduced chi-square, and compute LOD and LOQ.
Report an unknown's concentration with an uncertainty from first-order propagation, cross-checked by Monte Carlo and bootstrap resampling.
steps: Set up a Python environment with NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and pandas, and write a seeded simulator for detector counts (signal rate + background rate, chosen counting time).
Simulate 200 counting windows; plot the histogram against the Poisson PMF, and run a chi-square goodness-of-fit test.
Write the Poisson log-likelihood, find the MLE numerically and analytically, and get its standard error from the curvature.
Estimate the background rate from a few short runs with a Gamma prior; plot prior and posterior and compare the 95% credible and confidence intervals.
Simulate a five-standard calibration curve with realistic heteroscedastic noise (or load real data from a past lab notebook) and fit it by OLS; plot residuals.
Refit by weighted least squares; compare slopes, standard errors and the reduced chi-square, and compute LOD and LOQ.
Predict an unknown's concentration from three replicate signals and propagate the uncertainty with the first-order formula.
Check the propagated uncertainty by Monte Carlo (resampling the noise) and by bootstrapping the standards; explain any disagreement.
Write a two-page report (Jupyter notebook) stating each result with its uncertainty and the assumptions behind it.
project.stack: Python, NumPy, SciPy (stats, optimize), Matplotlib, pandas, Jupyter
